subsection: 8. The communist economies: problems and outcomes

notes.h: Background: communism, Sovietisation and the Cold War economic rivalry
notes.b: After 1945 Europe split into a capitalist west and a communist east, and the two sides competed over whose economic system could deliver more. To follow the problems of the communist economies, you first need the system they were built on and the dates of the leaders who ran it.
points: Communism, as used here, means one-party rule combined with a publicly owned, centrally planned economy, in which the state rather than private owners decides what is made and at what price.

Capitalism rests on private ownership, markets and profit, whereas communism rests on public ownership and state direction. This difference made the economy a central battleground of the Cold War, because each side claimed to offer people a better life.
After 1945 the Soviet Union dominated eastern Europe, and communist parties took power there in 1945–48. Sovietisation means remodelling these states, their economies included, on the Soviet pattern.

The Marshall Plan (1947) offered American aid to rebuild Europe and deepened the division of the continent, because the Soviet bloc refused Marshall aid and set up its own economic arrangements instead.

Stalin died in March 1953. Khrushchev then led the Soviet Communist Party from 1953 until he was removed in October 1964, Brezhnev led from 1964 to 1982 (he died in November 1982), and Gorbachev became General Secretary on 11 March 1985.
notes.tip: Exams use communist economic failure as a cause in questions on why communism collapsed in eastern Europe. Keep these leaders and dates to hand so that you can date every example you give.

notes.h: How Soviet central planning worked, and its origins
notes.b: Communist economies were run by central planning, in which the state set production targets and allocated resources instead of leaving decisions to markets. The system was built in the Soviet Union first, at enormous human cost.
points: Gosplan, the Soviet state planning committee (set up in 1921), drew up five-year plans that set output targets for industry, agriculture and trade. Prices were also set by the state, so there were no market signals telling factories what people wanted.
Priority was given to heavy industry (steel, coal, machinery and armaments), while consumer goods and housing were neglected, because the plans aimed to build industrial and military strength first.
Stalin's first Five-Year Plan began in 1928 and built heavy industry and cities at great human cost.

Collectivisation, the forcing of peasants to give up private farms and work in large state-controlled farms, was carried through in the Soviet Union in the early 1930s. Together with the famine of 1932–33 it killed millions, though estimates of the total vary widely.

Output was driven by pressing workers to exceed their norms (set work quotas). The Stakhanovite campaigns, which began in the Soviet Union in 1935 and were named after the miner Alexei Stakhanov, held up record-breaking workers as models, and they were copied in eastern Europe from the late 1940s.
notes.tip: For the planning system, name the body (Gosplan), the type of plan (five-year plans with gross output targets) and two effects such as heavy industry first and neglect of consumer goods and housing. These are the recurring Ordinary Level points.

notes.h: Exporting the model: nationalisation, Comecon and Soviet extraction
notes.b: Once communist parties held power in eastern Europe, the Soviet economic model was copied there. This tied the satellite economies, the states under Soviet influence, closely to Moscow.
points: In eastern Europe, industry, banks and large estates were nationalised (taken into state ownership) in 1945–48. Plans on the Soviet pattern followed from about 1949–51, for example Poland's Six-Year Plan (1950–55) and East Germany's first Five-Year Plan (1951).

Showpiece new industrial towns were built to symbolise the new system, such as Nowa Huta, a steel town and combine near Kraków begun in 1949, and Stalinstadt in East Germany, a steel town founded in 1950 and renamed Eisenhüttenstadt in 1961.

Collectivisation was imposed on most eastern European farms after 1945, and was pressed hard in Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria, Romania and East Germany. Poland was the major exception, because most Polish farms stayed in private hands.

Comecon, founded in January 1949 in Moscow (the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance), coordinated trade and planning among the Soviet bloc. It is usually seen as a Soviet answer to the Marshall Plan.

Comecon trade used a non-convertible accounting currency, one that could not be exchanged for Western money (bilateral clearing at first, then the transferable rouble from 1963), at prices set by planners.
In practice the Soviet Union supplied cheap raw materials and energy and took manufactured goods from the satellites. This is why the east European economies became dependent on Soviet supplies.

In the early years the Soviet Union also took resources out of the region through reparations (payments in goods) and Soviet-controlled joint companies in Hungary, Romania and East Germany in the late 1940s and early 1950s. In 1949–53 eastern Europe's trade shifted from the West to the Soviet Union.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the two stages of Sovietisation. The political takeover came in 1945–48, and the economic remodelling with Soviet-style plans came from about 1949–51.

notes.h: Problems of planning: shortages, poor quality and low innovation
notes.b: Central planning produced chronic shortages of goods, poor quality and slow adoption of new technology. Each problem had a cause in how the system rewarded managers, and together they undermined the economies over time.
points: Planners set targets in gross output terms, meaning the total quantity produced. This encouraged factories to produce heavy and low-quality goods rather than goods that consumers wanted, because quantity was what earned the reward.

Prices were fixed by the state rather than by supply and demand, so shortages in shops coexisted with surpluses of unwanted goods in warehouses. Nothing in the system adjusted production to what people would actually buy.
Shortages of consumer goods, meat, housing and cars were common, and long queues and black markets (illegal trade in scarce goods) were a permanent feature of daily life.

Innovation was slow because managers had little incentive to adopt new technology, and the state discouraged risk-taking. A manager who changed methods risked missing the target and gained little if the change worked.

Housing was built in standard blocks and was often overcrowded. In East Germany buyers had to wait many years for a car such as the Trabant, which shows how little the system answered consumer demand.
notes.tip: When you explain an effect such as shortages or poor quality, state its cause in the same sentence (fixed prices or gross output targets). Examiners reward effect plus cause, not a bare list.

notes.h: Problems of the system as a whole: farming, environment, extensive growth and the arms burden
notes.b: Beyond the daily shortages, the system had deeper structural weaknesses. Agriculture stayed unproductive, industry damaged the environment, growth depended on adding more inputs, and military spending drained resources.
points: Soviet agriculture remained unproductive, with a large share of the labour force employed on farms. The Soviet Union bought large amounts of Western grain after the poor harvest of 1963 and again in the 1970s.
Environmental damage was severe. Industrial regions such as northern Bohemia and Upper Silesia were polluted by heavy industry, and in the Aral Sea basin irrigation for cotton shrank the Aral Sea.

The economies relied on extensive growth, which comes from adding more labour and raw materials, and could not move to intensive growth, which comes from better technology and productivity. Once the supply of new workers dried up in the 1970s, growth slowed.

The arms race and the cost of maintaining an army and military industries absorbed a large share of national output, especially in the Soviet Union. This was at the cost of consumers and investment, because resources spent on weapons could not be spent on housing or modern factories.
notes.tip: Keep extensive growth (more inputs) and intensive growth (better productivity) apart. For the arms burden, say a large share of output and give no percentage, because estimates vary widely.

notes.h: Reform attempts in the Soviet Union: Khrushchev and Kosygin
notes.b: Soviet leaders knew the system performed badly, and tried to improve it without giving up central control. Both main reforms were partial, and neither lasted in its original form.
points: Khrushchev's reform of 1957 replaced industrial ministries with regional economic councils (sovnarkhozy), aiming to bring decisions closer to local industry. Ministries were restored after he fell in October 1964, so the reform was reversed.

Khrushchev also tried to lift the production of consumer goods and housing. He launched a mass housebuilding drive from the mid-1950s and in 1957 pledged to overtake the USA in output of goods such as meat, milk and butter, but this was not achieved.

Alexei Kosygin, Soviet prime minister from 1964 to 1980, announced his economic reform in September 1965. It gave enterprises more control over profits and pricing, but central control of investment stayed in place, and the reform also restored the ministries.

By the late 1960s Kosygin's reform had been watered down and it faded. A common explanation is that ministries and the party feared losing control, and the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 also discouraged further experiment.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the two reforms. Khrushchev in 1957 decentralised to regional councils, while Kosygin in 1965 gave enterprises more autonomy and restored the ministries.

notes.h: Reform attempts elsewhere: Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Yugoslavia
notes.b: Some bloc states went further than the Soviet Union in introducing market elements. Even so, none gave up one-party rule, which limited how far reform could go.
points: Czechoslovakia's New Economic Model of the mid-1960s was designed by the economist Ota Šik and proposed market mechanisms. The Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968 ended it, and also warned other bloc states against going too far.

Hungary's New Economic Mechanism came into force on 1 January 1968. It allowed limited market prices and private enterprise in services, and it survived in part into the 1980s, which made it a model of partial reform.

Hungary's policy under János Kádár, who led the country from 1956 to 1988, was nicknamed goulash communism. It tolerated small private plots and enterprises and gave citizens more consumer goods than in other bloc states.
Hungary's reforms gave managers more freedom and allowed a second economy, private work done after hours alongside the official one, but the state kept control of the main industries and prices.

Yugoslavia under Tito was expelled from the Cominform (the Soviet-led communist bloc organisation) in 1948. It left Soviet alignment and was never a full member of Comecon. From 1950 it developed worker self-management and market socialism, and it allowed its citizens to travel and work abroad.
Yugoslavia's system had costs. It ran up heavy foreign debt and suffered high inflation in the 1980s.
notes.tip: For a comparison question, say why Hungary went further than the Soviet Union (limited market prices and private services) and why even Hungary stayed within communism (the state kept the main industries and prices). Do not mix Polish and Hungarian leaders.

notes.h: Why reform stopped, and the Brezhnev era of stagnation
notes.b: Reforms stalled because they threatened the control of the party and the ministries. Under Leonid Brezhnev, who led from 1964 to 1982, the Soviet leadership avoided reform and the economy grew more slowly.
points: Fear of losing party and ministry control is a common explanation of why reforms stopped, and the 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia served as a warning of the risks of loosening central control.

Growth in the Soviet economy slowed in the 1970s, as the labour force grew more slowly and the rise in productivity fell. The period became known as stagnation (zastoi), a label applied later, especially by Gorbachev.

The Soviet Union earned large hard currency (convertible Western money) revenues from oil and gas exports after the oil price rises of 1973 and 1979. This let the leadership buy Western grain and technology and postpone reform.
When oil prices fell sharply in 1986 this support vanished, so the economy's weaknesses were exposed. Living standards for most people had improved only slowly during the 1970s.

Under Brezhnev the Soviet Union reached rough nuclear parity with the USA and increased its military spending, which took a large share of national output at the cost of consumer goods and investment. Soviet forces entered Afghanistan in December 1979, which added to the burden.
Rewarding party loyalty rather than performance led to corruption and an ageing leadership.
Consumers experienced shortages of basic goods. The black market, bribery and blat, the use of personal contacts and favours to obtain scarce goods and services, became part of ordinary life.
notes.tip: Explain stagnation with its cause: oil and gas revenue let the leadership postpone reform until the oil price fell in 1986.

notes.h: Poland: price rises, protest and Western debt
notes.b: Poland's attempts to raise living standards by borrowing from the West ended in debt and repeated waves of protest. Three price-rise crises, in December 1970, June 1976 and summer 1980, mark the story.
points: Price rises announced in December 1970 led to riots and strikes in Gdańsk, Gdynia and Szczecin on the Baltic coast. They brought the fall of Władysław Gomułka, who was replaced by Edward Gierek on 20 December 1970.
Gierek borrowed heavily from Western banks to finance imports of machinery and consumer goods. These were intended to modernise industry and win public support.
Price rises announced on 24 June 1976 led to strikes and riots, notably at Radom and Ursus. The government withdrew the increases the next day.

Gierek's strategy failed for several reasons. The new factories produced goods that were not competitive in Western markets, so export earnings did not pay off the loans, and agricultural output suffered from a lack of investment.
Poland's debt to the West was over 20 billion dollars by 1980. By then it had become unsustainable, the economy had shrunk and shops were bare of meat.

Price rises announced on 1 July 1980 set off strikes that spread to Gdańsk in August. The shipyard strike there began in mid-August, the Gdańsk Agreement was signed on 31 August 1980, and Solidarity, led by Lech Wałęsa, was founded in September 1980.
Poland's economic crisis was a cause of Solidarity, and the economic collapse in the 1980s helped to bring the communists to the Round Table talks with Solidarity, which began in February 1989.
notes.tip: Examiners want the three crises with dates and what followed each, and Western debt as the reason Gierek's plan failed. Keep Gomułka (fell 1970) and Gierek (1970–80) apart from Kádár of Hungary.

notes.h: Gorbachev and perestroika: reform that came too late
notes.b: Mikhail Gorbachev tried to rescue the Soviet economy by restructuring it. His reforms weakened the old system without putting a working new one in its place.
points: Gorbachev launched perestroika, meaning restructuring of the economy, in 1986 (27th Party Congress, February–March 1986). It coincided with falling oil prices in 1986, which cut the Soviet Union's hard currency earnings.
The Law on State Enterprise, passed in 1987 and in force from 1988, gave factories more freedom. The 1988 law on cooperatives allowed private business.
These laws weakened central control without creating a functioning market. Planners no longer directed supply reliably, but prices and competition did not yet replace them.
By 1989–90 the Soviet economy was suffering from shortages, a growing budget deficit and falling output, and rationing (coupons) for basic goods appeared in several cities.
notes.tip: Perestroika is the economic reform and glasnost is openness, so write about perestroika only and name its failure: control was loosened but no market took its place.

notes.h: The East–West gap and the legacy of the communist economies
notes.b: By the late 1980s the gap between the communist states and the West was plain to see, and several bloc economies survived only on Western credit or severe austerity. Their end left problems for the successor states.
points: Romania under Nicolae Ceaușescu announced in 1989 that its foreign debt was repaid. The cost was cuts in imports and in food, heating and electricity for the population, who suffered shortages.

East Germany was the strongest industrial economy in the bloc by common assessment, but it depended on West German credit and trade concessions, including a billion-mark loan arranged in 1983, with a second in 1984.
The German economic, monetary and social union of 1 July 1990 exposed East German industries to competition and led to mass closures.

The gap with the West was visible by 1989. East German and Czechoslovak citizens could see how much better West Germans and Austrians lived on television and through travel, and living standards in the Soviet Union lagged far behind.
The end of the Soviet bloc's economic system left a legacy of obsolete industry, environmental damage and unemployment that the successor states had to address.
notes.tip: The strongest essay answers link shortages, debt, the East–West gap and the loss of Soviet will to prop up the system as causes of the collapse in 1989.

notes.b: The bloc was not uniform, and examiners reward comparison of different states. Each started from a different level of development and handled planning differently.
points: Czechoslovakia was the most industrialised state in the region before the war, because the Czech lands were the industrial heartland of the Habsburg Empire and of interwar Czechoslovakia.
Czechoslovakia's living standards were among the highest in the bloc in the 1950s, but it stagnated under rigid planning in the 1960s and was the home of Ota Šik's reform.

East Germany was among the most advanced economies in the bloc and the showcase of socialism, but it lost skilled workers to the West until the Berlin Wall was built in August 1961, after millions of people had left since 1949.

Bulgaria and Romania were still largely agricultural in 1945 and were industrialised rapidly. Romania developed heavy industry, oil and chemicals and pursued an independent foreign policy under Ceaușescu.
Ceaușescu's Romania exported food and fuel to pay its debts and rationed food and electricity in the 1980s. His systematisation programme, announced in 1988, planned to demolish villages.

Hungary's partial reforms and Poland's private farming made those states more flexible than the Soviet Union. However, their dependence on Western credit made them vulnerable when interest rates and prices rose around 1980.
notes.tip: A single-country narrative scores lower than a thematic answer with dated examples from several states, so use these contrasts to compare.

notes.h: Assessment: achievements and failures of communist economies
notes.b: Communist economies achieved rapid industrialisation and social welfare, but they failed to sustain growth or satisfy consumers. Judgement answers need both sides and a clear verdict.
points: Achievements: rapid industrialisation, near-universal literacy, free health care and education, full employment including high employment of women, and cheap housing and basic goods.
Limits: chronic shortages, low quality, poor housing, environmental damage and a standard of living that fell further behind the West.
Eastern Europe's communist states did expand education, cheap housing and health care, but their living standards fell behind West European levels by the 1970s.
Contemporary Western accounts often stressed the failure of the planned economy, while Soviet and bloc officials emphasised the achievements of industrialisation and social welfare.
Later historians stress both the system's real successes in mobilising resources and the structural limits that made it impossible to sustain growth without political reform.
The final judgement of historians is that the planned economy could build basic industry, but could not adapt to the information-based economies of the 1980s.
Reform within the bloc was partial, because leaders would not give up party control. Economic failure was one cause, not the only cause, of the events of 1989.
notes.tip: State a clear verdict and name one cause of long-run decline, which scores above simply listing achievements and failures. Set achievements (industrialisation, welfare, full employment) against failures (shortages, environment, falling behind).

keyTerms.definition: A political and economic system in which a single communist party directs the state and the economy is publicly owned and centrally planned.
The process by which communist parties backed by the Soviet Union took control of eastern European states and remodelled their economies on the Soviet pattern.
The system in which the state sets production targets and allocates resources through plans, rather than through market prices.
The Council for Mutual Economic Assistance, founded in January 1949, which coordinated trade and planning among the Soviet bloc states.
A plan setting output targets for the economy over five years, the central instrument of Soviet-style planning.
The informal name for the more relaxed, consumer-oriented policies of Kádár's Hungary, which allowed limited private enterprise.
The merging of private farms into large state or collective farms run under central plans.
The name given to the Brezhnev years, when Soviet economic growth slowed and reform was avoided.
Gorbachev's programme of restructuring the Soviet economy, begun in 1986, which introduced limited private enterprise and enterprise freedom.
The unofficial private work, trade and services that grew up alongside the planned economy in communist states, especially in Hungary.
